title: Probability, with perspective.
description: Two short lectures on changing the reference group, reading probabilities, and testing independence.
notice: Synthetic demonstration · These are self-authored sample handouts, not real teacher materials.

glossary.definition: The probability of an event within a specified conditioning event of positive probability.
glossary.plain_language: Keep only the students who meet the condition, then ask what share of that group has the property of interest.
glossary.example: In the 100-student survey, 24 of the 40 statistics students take economics: P(E | S) = 24/40 = 0.60. The conditioning group is nonempty.

confused_with.distinction: The same 24 students take both subjects, but P(E | S) uses the 40 statistics students as its denominator; P(E ∩ S) uses all 100 students and equals 0.24.
P(E | S) = 0.60 counts economics within statistics students; P(E) = 0.50 counts economics across all 100 students. Compare these to test independence when P(S) > 0.

glossary.definition: The probability that both events occur.
glossary.plain_language: Count the students who satisfy both descriptions, then compare them with everyone in the survey.
glossary.example: Twenty-four of all 100 students take both economics and statistics: P(E ∩ S) = 24/100 = 0.24.

confused_with.distinction: Joint P(E ∩ S) = 0.24 asks about both subjects in the whole survey; conditional P(E | S) = 0.60 asks about economics within the statistics group.
Joint probability requires both E and S, giving 24/100. Marginal P(E) includes economics students outside S as well, giving 50/100.

glossary.definition: The group used as the denominator when calculating a proportion.
glossary.plain_language: Name the whole group for your question before deciding which count belongs in the denominator.
glossary.example: “Among statistics students” selects the 40 students in S. The other 60 survey participants stay outside this question’s denominator.

glossary.definition: Two events are independent when their joint probability equals the product of their probabilities.
glossary.plain_language: Knowing that one event happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged, when the conditioning event has positive probability.
glossary.example: In this survey, P(E | S) = 0.60 differs from P(E) = 0.50, so E and S are not independent. The equivalent product check also fails: 0.24 ≠ 0.50 × 0.40 = 0.20.

glossary.definition: The probability of an event without conditioning on the other event in a joint distribution.
glossary.plain_language: Ask about one event across the whole survey, without restricting to the other event.
glossary.example: Fifty of all 100 students take economics, whether or not they take statistics: P(E) = 50/100 = 0.50.

confused_with.distinction: Marginal P(E) uses all 100 students; conditional P(E | S) uses only the 40 statistics students. Their economics counts are 50 and 24, respectively.
P(E) counts all 50 economics students; P(E ∩ S) counts only the 24 who take both subjects. Both are shares of all 100 students.
